analysis.one_liner: Bans Medicare drug-plan middlemen from earning fees tied to drug prices or rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill had bipartisan backing from six senators — including the Senate Finance chairman and ranking member — but was referred to that committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) — the middlemen that negotiate drug coverage for Medicare drug plans — get paid. PBMs could charge only a flat service fee, with no income tied to drug prices, discounts, or rebates, and would have to hand back any extra money to Medicare. Plans and PBMs would have to certify each year that they are following the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries in prescription drug plans. Today, PBMs can earn fees calculated as a percentage of a drug's list price, which gives them a reason to prefer costlier drugs, and they can profit on the gap between what they pay pharmacies and what plans pay them. Banning price-linked pay removes those incentives, which should push down plan costs and premiums and steer formularies toward cheaper drugs [S2][S3]. The public fisc also benefits, since any excess PBM income must be disgorged to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires PBMs serving Medicare Part D prescription drug plans to be paid only a flat, bona fide service fee that is not based on drug prices, discounts, rebates, or any other remuneration — including fees passed on by affiliates, subsidiaries, or agents.
Forces PBMs to disgorge to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services any money they received outside the flat fee, and requires both plans and PBMs to certify compliance with the rules annually.

Removes the built-in incentive for PBMs to favor higher-priced drugs: because PBM pay can no longer be a percentage of a drug's list price or contingent on rebates, the middleman no longer profits when a more expensive drug is chosen.

Applies even when the drug plan's own insurer is acting as the PBM or the PBM sits downstream of the plan, closing the most obvious workaround; the bill also makes clear plans themselves may still accept rebates that lower net costs.

analysis.who_pays: The PBM industry, dominated by three companies — CVS Caremark, Express Scripts (Cigna), and Optum Rx (UnitedHealth) — would give up revenue earned from price-linked administrative fees, spread pricing, and rebate-based compensation. Their parent insurers, which mostly own the PBMs, would absorb the loss. Drug plans would continue paying for PBM services, but as flat fees that reflect fair market value rather than a share of drug spending. Medicare beneficiaries would not directly pay anything under the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and parent insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage drug coverage. PBMs would keep their price-linked and rebate-based pay in the far larger employer and commercial insurance markets, limiting the real-world impact on the industry's business model.

It does not cap drug prices or force disclosure of rebate negotiations. Plans, not patients, would still receive manufacturer rebates, so whether savings reach beneficiaries at the pharmacy counter depends on what plans and PBMs negotiate next.

Enforcement rests on annual self-certification by the plans and PBMs themselves, plus whatever oversight the Secretary of Health and Human Services designs, with no independent audit mechanism written into the bill.
Flat fees must reflect fair market value for services; if PBMs reprice their fees upward to replace lost rebate income, drug plans could face higher administrative costs that flow into premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a good one for Medicare beneficiaries: the bill targets a specific, well-documented conflict — middlemen earning more when drugs cost more — and it applies to affiliates and vertically integrated insurers, where the incentives actually live. But it is a narrow strike, not a comprehensive fix: it leaves the commercial market untouched, keeps rebates flowing to plans rather than patients, and relies on self-certification. An honest supporter would call it a meaningful first step for the one market where Congress directly sets the rules, while acknowledging PBMs' business model would largely survive outside Medicare.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Menendez introduced the bill on June 14, 2023 with an unusual showing of six original sponsors split evenly between the parties, including Senate Finance Chairman Ron Wyden and the committee's ranking Republican Mike Crapo.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day — the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare — and no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

Seven senators had signed on as cosponsors by the end (four Republicans, three Democrats), yet the bill never received a committee markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

Across the same period, PBM reform was one of the most active areas of health policy debate in Congress, with multiple competing bills and hearings — making the complete inaction on this particular bill notable rather than a sign of thin interest in the topic.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The three dominant pharmacy benefit managers — CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and Optum Rx — and the insurers that own them. They kept their price-linked fees and rebate-based compensation in Medicare untouched, and in every other market, because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The big three PBMs and their insurers

for.name: Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of six original cosponsors spanning the Finance Committee's leadership.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor of the bill; the committee he chairs took no action on it.

for.name: Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor, giving the bill the endorsement of both party leaders on the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare.

for.name: Marsha Blackburn, Jon Tester, Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Joined as the other three original sponsors, making the introduction evenly split between three Democrats and three Republicans.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote at any point in the two-year Congress, despite the chair and ranking member both being cosponsors.

against.name: The major pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
against.what_they_did: The three companies that process roughly four out of five U.S. prescriptions fought a broad campaign against PBM reform legislation during this period through lobbying and public relations.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was evenly split — three Democrats and three Republicans among original sponsors, finishing with seven cosponsors (4 R, 3 D) — yet it still never received a vote.

industries.note: The bill directly targets how PBMs get paid in Medicare: flat fees only, no price-linked fees, spreads, or rebate-based income, plus disgorgement of anything collected improperly. PBMs earn more when drugs cost more under current arrangements, so their gain has come at beneficiaries' and taxpayers' expense.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated insurers (CVS Health/Aetna, Cigna/Evernorth, UnitedHealth/Optum)
industries.note: These insurers own the big PBMs, so the bill's fee restrictions hit their consolidated revenue. But the bill explicitly lets drug plan sponsors acting as their own PBM keep rebates that lower net costs, softening the blow on the insurance side of the house.
Plans must certify compliance and would negotiate flat PBM fees, adding administrative structure. In exchange, they keep the right to accept manufacturer rebates that reduce their net drug costs.

Pharmacies have long complained that PBM reimbursement practices and spread pricing squeeze their margins and push them to close. Decoupling PBM pay from drug prices reduces the incentive to steer volume and game reimbursement, though the bill does not regulate pharmacy reimbursement directly.
